Today's big story: Anthropic Below Its IPO Price: Do Giants Come Back?

Qualcomm stock rose 10.3% on Monday, November 23, 2026. The S&P 500 gained 4.7% the same session.

There was no earnings report or SEC filing from the company around the move. The rise came with the whole chip group. All 33 other semiconductor companies worth $2 billion or more rose on Monday.

What Happened In Chip Stocks On Monday?

The biggest chip news came from NVIDIA. Its board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive on November 23, effective immediately. NVIDIA stock rose 31.5% that session.

Monday's rise came one session after a rough Friday for Qualcomm.

Qualcomm fell 7.5% on Friday, November 20, then rose 10.3% on Monday. Swings that size are hard to sit through when you live on the income from your savings. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500's, from 50 companies that have paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row. See what it pays.

Qualcomm's own tie to AI runs through a young data center business. On the November 4 earnings call, management said the data center business "is off to a strong start." It added that its guidance for the current quarter "reflects the commencement of shipments to 2 hyperscaler customers."

Hyperscalers are the largest cloud computing companies.

Was It Qualcomm Or Its Group?

It was the group. Among the other semiconductor companies worth $2 billion or more, the median gain was 14.1%. In all, 29 of the 33 rose by 5% or more. Qualcomm rose with its group, but its 10.3% gain was well below that 14.1% median.

Every company on Trefis's peer list for Qualcomm rose too. They are NVIDIA, Intel, Texas Instruments, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom. Intel gained 16.3%, while Broadcom rose 3%.

Where Does Qualcomm Stock Stand After The Rise?

A rise like this is not rare for Qualcomm. It had 4 sessions with a rise at least this large in the past year. The latest session with a move this large in either direction was a fall of 11.1% on October 30.

Monday's close of $165.38 sits well below its highest close of the past 12 months, $251.02 on May 29. The past six months were hard. From the May 26 close, Qualcomm lost 32.9% including dividends, while the S&P 500 lost 3.2%. For how deep its falls have run, see How Big Could Qualcomm Stock's Next Fall Be?

The stock trades at 4.1 times its sales of the past year, a measure called the price-to-sales ratio. The S&P 500 as a whole trades at 3.1 times sales.

Today's big story: Anthropic Below Its IPO Price: Do Giants Come Back?

Nvidia stock rose 31.5% on Monday, Nov 23, 2026. The S&P 500 gained 4.7% the same day. The rise came the day the company said its board had reinstated Jensen Huang as president and chief executive. All 33 other semiconductor companies worth $2 billion or more also gained, with a median rise of 13.2%.

What did Nvidia announce on Monday?

The company said Huang was back as president, chief executive and board member, effective immediately. It filed an 8-K, the form a company uses to report a major event, the same day.

The gain followed a hard week. Nvidia fell in each of the five sessions before. The last was a 14% drop on Friday, Nov 20. For that fall, see What Sent NVIDIA Stock Lower On Friday?

In two sessions, Nvidia fell 14% and then rose 31.5%. If your savings have to cover your bills, swings that size are hard to live with. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500's, from 50 companies that have paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row. See what it pays.

Monday's news reversed a step taken earlier this month. On Nov 12, the board announced that Huang had resigned. On the Nov 17 earnings call, the board's chairman said the board "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." For more on that exit, see Does Huang's Exit Sink Nvidia Stock? History Is Split.

The business kept growing through the change. On that call, the company reported quarterly revenue of $116 billion. It said revenue "more than doubled year-over-year."

Did Nvidia rise on its own or with chip stocks?

It rose with its group, but much further. Its sub-industry is semiconductors. The other companies in it worth $2 billion or more had a median gain of 13.2%. Of those 33, 29 gained 5% or more. The technology sector fund XLK rose 9%.

All five companies on Trefis's peer list for Nvidia rose as well. They are Advanced Micro Devices, Intel, Broadcom, Qualcomm and Marvell Technology. Marvell gained the most, 18.4%, and Broadcom the least, 3%.

Where does Nvidia stock stand after the jump?

No session in the prior year saw Nvidia move this much in either direction. Its biggest earlier move in that time was Friday's 14% fall.

Monday's close was $165.05, up from $125.53 on Friday. That Friday close was the lowest of the past twelve months. The highest was $239.24, on Oct 6. Over the past twelve months, the stock returned -8.4% including dividends. The S&P 500 returned 12%.

At Monday's close, Nvidia's market value was 13.2 times its sales of the four quarters to July 2026. Those four quarters leave out the $116 billion quarter reported on Nov 17. The S&P 500 as a whole trades at 3.1 times its sales.

title: How Nvidia's Jensen Huang Survived the Kind of Scandal That Ends CEO Careers
detail:
How Nvidia's Jensen Huang Survived the Kind of Scandal That Ends CEO Careers
Daragh Thomas
Wed, November 25, 2026 at 12:55 PM CST 3 min read
NVDA
MCD
INTC
BP
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Benzinga and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue on some items through the links below.

Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang got his job back on Monday after resigning amid reports of undisclosed relationships with employees.

Other CEOs haven't been so fortunate. Similar scandals have ended careers at McDonald's, BP and Intel, costing some executives tens of millions of dollars in compensation.

When Office Romances End Careers

McDonald's (NYSE:MCD) fired Steve Easterbrook in 2019 over a consensual relationship with an employee. After discovering additional undisclosed relationships, the company sued Easterbrook and recovered more than $105 million in cash and equity awards.

In 2023, BP (NYSE:BP) CEO Bernard Looney resigned after failing to fully disclose relationships with colleagues. The oil giant concluded that Looney had knowingly misled its board, costing him up to £32.4 million (about $41 million) in compensation.

Even Nvidia's own industry has a precedent. Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) then-CEO Brian Krzanich resigned in 2018 after an investigation found that a consensual relationship with an employee violated company policy.

The Rules He Helped Write

Separate from the national security concerns surrounding Huang's resignation, The New York Times reported on Nov. 11 that he had a relationship with Nvidia's healthcare vice president, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him.

At Tuesday's employee meeting, Huang acknowledged violating company policies and said he had written much of Nvidia's code of conduct himself. He argued that a breach should not automatically lead to dismissal, WIRED reported.

"It has to always be evaluated in the context of the human," Huang said.

Wall Street's Trillion-Dollar Exception

Nvidia shares lost nearly a third of their value after the scandal broke. Monday's rally added back nearly $1 trillion in market value, though the stock was still down 17% from its pre-scandal price as of Tuesday's close.

The wider AI industry relies on Nvidia for both chips and financing, and investors had feared Huang's departure could disrupt it. Even Jay Goldberg, a Seaport Research Partners analyst and longtime Nvidia bear, put it bluntly.

"There's no one that can really replace Jensen. I mean, he does the roles of like several people," he previously told Benzinga.

Who Pays the Price?

In July last year, Astronomer CEO Andy Byron and human resources chief Kristin Cabot both resigned after a camera caught them embracing at a Coldplay concert.

Byron landed another executive role this month, while Cabot has yet to find another job, Bloomberg reported.

Trump Says It's "Probably Not Too Late" for a US Stake in Nvidia. That's a Big Risk for Its Multiple ©Nickel_Bell from Getty Images and Изображения пользователя Axel Makhalov via Canva
Key Takeaways

President Trump told the New York Post it's "probably not too late" for a US stake in Nvidia like the 9.9% stake the government took in Intel last year.

The talk adds a governance discount to NVIDIA's multiple on top of the discount from Jensen Huang's brief exit.

Analysts expect normalized EPS to more than triple in two years, yet NVIDIA trades at 11x forward earnings, against a five-year average of 35x.

NVIDIA needs no money from Washington, so a stake would bring only the government's priorities.

NVIDIA (NVDA:NASDAQ) got its CEO back on Monday with help from the White House. Now the White House is talking about owning a piece of the company.

President Trump told the New York Post, in an interview published Tuesday, that he has thought about a US stake in NVIDIA like the one the government took in Intel (INTC:NASDAQ) last year:

"I thought about it. I said, 'You know, maybe I should do it,' but I didn't bring it up at this point. It's probably not too late."

The Wall Street Journal's Greg Ip had already said what that relationship looks like: "Like the original government-sponsored enterprises, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, Nvidia's mission and governance are now effectively steered by the federal government. Huang owes his job to Trump."

Short seller Jim Chanos posted on X on the day NVIDIA's board brought Huang back: "Just a reminder that industries dependent on government intervention/bailouts don't usually trade at premium valuations."

That's a problem for a stock whose multiple has already taken a beating.

TIKR tracks 63 analysts on Nvidia. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Nvidia, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Nvidia's Analyst Ratings

Wall Street's estimates keep climbing

The discount has nothing to do with the business. Analysts expect normalized EPS to more than triple, from $4.77 in the fiscal year that ended in January to $16.61 in the year ending January 2028:

Nvidia (NVDA): normalized EPS, actual and consensus estimates, $ per share, fiscal 2024-2028 (years to January) (TIKR)

The stock hasn't kept up. NVIDIA trades at 11x forward earnings, against a five-year average of 35x and a peak of 70x in May 2023:

Nvidia (NVDA): forward (NTM) P/E, last 5 years (TIKR)

Its five-year low of 8.7x came on Nov. 20, while Huang was out of the job. Now that he's back, that discount should start to shrink. A government stake would add a different discount, and that one may not go away.

Washington already has a say in NVIDIA's business

NVIDIA's outlook already assumes no China data center compute revenue. And Jefferies estimates that Commerce's remote-access rule puts $44 billion to $62 billion of NVIDIA's data center revenue at risk next year.

Trump says "maybe I should" have Washington buy Nvidia stock, and an Intel-style 10% stake would be worth about $380 billion.

Nvidia needs no bailout, generating over $40 billion in quarterly free cash flow, so new shares issued to Washington would dilute investors.

Washington regulates Nvidia's China chip exports, so owning a stake would pit taxpayer returns against national security priorities.

Read: Building a portfolio and living off one are two completely different skills, and almost nobody teaches the second. This problem is what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps with, and it is free today. Read more here.

Washington is rewriting the rules of American capitalism. After decades of using tax breaks, subsidies, and government contracts to support strategically important industries, the federal government is increasingly interested in becoming a shareholder in the businesses it helps.

Shutterstock

For investors, government ownership introduces a new variable into the investment equation. Uncle Sam has priorities that don't always align with those of Wall Street, particularly when national security and economic competitiveness are involved.

Now President Donald Trump is entertaining the possibility of taking a government stake in Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA). Applying the same ownership model Washington used with another American chipmaker could result in a government holding worth $380 billion.

Washington Wants a Piece of the AI Boom

In an interview with the New York Post yesterday, Trump acknowledged he had considered having the federal government acquire Nvidia stock, saying, "Maybe I should do it." Although he hasn't raised the issue with the company, he added, "It's probably not too late."

The comments follow Trump's intervention in Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO, underscoring how closely Washington now ties America's artificial intelligence (AI) leadership to the fortunes of one corporation.

There is already a blueprint for such an investment. In August 2025, the Trump administration secured a 9.9% ownership stake in Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) in exchange for $8.9 billion. The investment comprised $5.7 billion in previously awarded CHIPS Act grants and $3.2 billion earmarked for the government's Secure Enclave program.
